en: Preface to the Records of the Dharma Assembly:
During the Eastern Jin dynasty, Master Huiyuan, together with the recluses Liu Yimin, Lei Cizong, Zong Bing, and other worthies, formed a religious society at Donglin.
On each of the six fasting days, they expounded the Way, engaging one another in inquiry and debate to investigate and clarify Buddhist principles, thereby serving as provisions for the Pure Land.

This is Master Ling’s "Flying Cane at White Clouds. On the day of the vegetarian feast, he also gathered various virtuous ones to engage in discourse from east to west, whether concerning Chan or the Teachings.
He did not withhold his analytical exposition; it was clear, simple, and easy to understand, as if pointing directly at one's palm. This is just like the World-Honored One...
For forty-nine years, he preached the Dharma according to the capacities of his audience; even his final act of holding up a flower before the assembly was not an error.

Was this not the Master’s compassionate heart reaching its limit, descending into the weeds to seek out those capable of receiving the truth? Since my youth, I have been fond of the Inner Canon, yet I remained stuck in intellectual interpretations of the texts.
It was only after thirty years of experiencing the vicissitudes of fortune and misfortune that I finally attained a profound realization, which remains vivid to me even today.

Yet sleep and food accompany me even through circumstances of misfortune, regret, sorrow, and anxiety—namely, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
thus, all manner of sufferings converge upon me. Nevertheless, the True Zhang Yizhan shall certainly not undergo such suffering.
My Master, moved by compassion, has frequently bestowed upon me the carved printing blocks of the scriptures and the names of the ancient virtuous masters.

He said: "I believe he knows the contents of my mind; when presented with the Buddha's words, he will certainly read them, and having read them, he will surely finish the entire volume without forgetting it.
This is what is meant by 'further employing diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting [the truth].'"
Record of the Yunshan Dharma Assembly:
Chan Master Weilín Speaking to the Upāsaka Disciples (Xi Dàcái, Pán Dàojìng, and Huáng Dàguǎng), Recorded Together by the Master.
The Master said: "Today, gathering here with you gentlemen, we shall engage in various conversations to establish the karmic conditions for Prajñā."
Not knowing where to begin, he remained silent for a long while and then said: "The body of the pure dharma-realm fundamentally has no appearing or disappearing.
Through the power of great compassionate vows, it manifests birth. Since I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, attained enlightenment, countless aeons as numerous as motes of dust have already passed.
This present appearance is not for any other purpose, but solely for the sake of the one great matter: that is to say, the desire..."
To cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Yet sentient beings are originally Buddhas;

this knowledge and vision is inherently possessed by the Buddhas. It is only because no one has opened it up for them that they have no means to awaken and enter it. Therefore, throughout beginningless kalpas, [they have remained thus].
Moment by moment, sentient beings only open their own limited perceptions; they create karma and undergo retribution, sinking into the cycle of birth and death with no means of escape.
Out of great compassion that identifies with them, the World-Honored One gives rise to deep pity and appears in the world by virtue of his vows. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"At that time, the World-Honored One, with the unobstructed eye of pure wisdom, universally observed all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, seeing that each of them possesses..."
The Tathāgata’s wisdom, virtue, and marks are not realized only because of delusive thoughts, inverted views, and attachments.
If one is free from delusive thoughts, then all-knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge will immediately manifest before them.

I shall instruct you in the noble path to cause you to leave behind delusive thoughts, so that within your own body you may perceive the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is no different from that of the Buddha.

It is different. Thus, at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he manifested the attainment of perfect awakening and, for the sake of the great beings whose faculties were matured, as well as the eight classes of gods, nāgas, and others, he preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in accordance with the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, for a certain class of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who, though present in the assembly, were like the deaf and the blind—neither seeing nor hearing—he cast off his precious robes to don tattered rags and manifested the six-foot form of Śākyamuni.
In the Deer Park, for those of inferior faculties, he differentiated and taught the One Buddha Vehicle as three:
namely, he taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the Śrāvaka vehicle; he taught the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;

and he taught the six perfections through provisional means for the Bodhisattvas of the expedient vehicles. Upon reaching the Vaipulya [sūtras], he then extensively expounded the Mahāyāna for all Bodhisattvas.

The various sutras employ skillful means to entice those of the Hīnayāna and lead them into the Mahāyāna; furthermore, through the manifold methods of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they refine and wash away their attachment to dharmas.

This process continues until the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where provisional teachings are opened up and the ultimate reality is revealed, unifying the three vehicles into one. As it is said:
"Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third. This is for the sake of the śrāvaka disciples.
He bestowed the prophecy of their attainment of Buddhahood, which extends to this very day; even those who possess mere faith and understanding are included within that prophecy.
Having completed his work of appearing in the world, he then proclaimed his entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Viewed in this light, from beginning to end, the Tathāgata employed various skillful means—whether provisional or ultimate, partial or complete—to preach immeasurable dharmas, all of which were for the sake of sentient beings.
This shatters all deluded thoughts and causes one to perceive the Buddha-nature; it is not for any other purpose. Indeed, the body, mind, world, and all phenomena are nothing but delusion.
If one can realize that delusion is fundamentally empty—not made empty by some external agent—and know that reality is fundamentally present.
"It is not something newly acquired; rather, it is entering into the Buddha-dharma.
One might say they are close to it. The Master said: "One day the World-Honored One ascended the seat and held up a single golden *pāla* flower to show the assembly.
Among the hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, none could fathom it. Only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said:"
I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, the subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate of the true mark which is formless.
It does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside the teachings, entrusted to Mahākāśyapa to be propagated for future generations so that it shall never be severed.
The source of the Chan school’s principle of not establishing written words, of directly pointing to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha, begins here.

For forty-nine years, the World-Honored One employed language and writing to expound upon the provisional and the real, the sudden and the gradual, according to the capacities of his listeners; yet he had not yet fully expressed his original intent.

Arriving at this point, he brings it forth face-to-face, manifesting the whole body in the present moment. Only those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence can suddenly perceive and suddenly awaken.
Only upon such realization is one truly fit to receive and uphold [the Dharma]. Kāśyapa transmitted it to the Second Patriarch, Ānanda; Ānanda transmitted it to the Third Patriarch, Śaṇakavāsin;
the Third Patriarch transmitted it to the Fourth Patriarch, Upagupta; and so on, down to the twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma.
Seeing that my Eastern Land possessed a vessel capable of holding the Mahāyāna Dharma, he specifically crossed the sea to come here. Thus, he became the [first] patriarch of the Eastern Land.

The First Patriarch first met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty; when the Emperor questioned him regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they did not accord, so he secretly crossed the Yangtze River to the Wei kingdom.
He resided at Shaolin for nine years, sitting all day long facing a wall. Later, he received the Second Patriarch, Shen Guang.
He severed his arm to find peace of mind; through prostration, he attained the marrow of the Dharma. Consequently, the robe and the teaching were entrusted to him. There is a verse that says:
"I have come to this land to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower opens into five petals; the fruition is naturally accomplished. As for what is called "transmitting the Dharma":
This is the transmission of the Dharma of the One Mind. There is no separate dharma outside of one's own mind that can be transmitted;

it is merely for the sake of others to untangle their attachments, loosen their bonds, turn from delusion toward awakening, and cause them to see their own nature—this is what is meant by "transmission.

The Second Patriarch transmitted it to the Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan; the Third Patriarch transmitted it to the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin; the Fourth Patriarch transmitted it to the Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren.
The Master [said]: "The Fifth Patriarch transmitted [the Dharma] to the Sixth Patriarch, Great Master Huineng. At eighty years of age, the Sixth Patriarch became a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend).

He demonstrated that he was illiterate, yet he exclusively opened the Dharma-gate of realizing the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). His Way shook the world. Yongjia said: 'The transmission of the robe through six generations is heard throughout the world;
those who have attained the Way among his descendants are beyond counting. Under the gate of Caoxi, those who attained the Way were like a forest. First...
Since the time of the Dharma [Bodhidharma], the transmission has been from one person to another alone until it reached the Sixth Patriarch, at which point the robe and bowl were discontinued.
His Dharma was transmitted universally. He had two great disciples: the first was Qingyuan Si, and the second was Nanyue Rang. From Rang emerged Mazu Daoyi;
from Mazu emerged more than eighty virtuous teachers (kalyāṇamitra). His great disciple was Baizhang Huaihai; from Huaihai emerged...
There were two [masters]: the first was Huishan Daoyou, and the second was Huangbo Xiyun. From Xiyun emerged Linji Yixuan, who founded the Linji school.
From Daoyou emerged Yangshan Huiji, who founded the Guiyang (Huichang) school. Qingyuan Xingsi gave rise to Shitou Xiqian. Shitou had two great disciples:
the first was Tianhuang Daowu, and the second was Yaoshan Weiyan. From Weiyan emerged Yunyan.
Sheng. Sheng was a successor of Dongshan Jia; Jia was a successor of Caoshan Ji. This constitutes the Cao-Dong school. Tianhuang was a successor of Longtan Xin;
Xin was a successor of Deshan Jian; Jian was a successor of Xuefeng Cun. Xuefeng Cun had two great disciples: one was Yunmen Yan, who founded the Yunmen school;
the other was Xuansha Bei. Bei was a successor of Dizang Chen; Chen was a successor of... [text continues].

Fayan Yi was the founder of the Fayan school. Although the five schools differ in their methods for engaging people's capacities, they are all nothing other than the elucidation of the World-Honored One’s "single flower held up" point—directly pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha.
Among them, the three schools of Weiyang, Yunmen, and Fayan ended with the Song dynasty; transmitted to this day, there remain only Linji and Caodong.
The two schools of the Chan tradition have declined; we now dwell in the age of the Final Dharma, when the faculties of people are inferior.

Students lack any genuine resolve for life and death, and they seldom possess authentic spiritual lineage. They concern themselves solely with the pursuit of fame and profit through the fly-whisk, making strife and contention over "self" and "others" their primary business.
This has filled the villages and neighborhoods, becoming a prevailing trend and a common custom. As my late teacher once said: "Today, Linji’s school has failed."
Linji did not wait for Caodong to condemn him; nor did Caodong become Caodong by waiting for Linji to condemn him.
These words encompass it all. When a man of resolve hears these words, who would endure them with such heartache and distress?
We only hope that there will be an extraordinary practitioner within the Dharma-gate who, before Śākyamuni appeared in Western India, [realizes the truth].
To manifest in the eastern lands of the future, before one has even entered the womb of one's parents, one must take a single look and see through it all:
"What are Śākyamuni, the Dharma, and oneself? They are but a mirage and empty flowers.

Only then is it well to shoulder this burden here with a naked body, so as to perhaps turn back the corrupt and evil winds of the final dharma age. If there be no such person, then what is called the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) [will perish].
This has been swept away entirely; what more is there to say? It is further said: "Those who study the Buddha-dharma study the supramundane dharma.

If one harbors even a single thought of mundane dharma, then despite diligent and arduous cultivation, one will remain entangled in the delusions of mundane dharma—discussing the profound and expounding the subtle—and have no connection whatsoever with the Buddha-dharma. One must believe that this one thing alone is the transcendence."
Regarding the causal conditions for the great matters of the world, one must first prepare a set of mind and conduct that transcend the mundane before being fit to enter the gate.
That we, this assembly today, burn incense and sit in stillness to engage in discussion for a short while is something that ordinary people of the world do not possess.
Master Fu said: "The people of the world cherish gold; I cherish a moment of stillness. Abundant gold disturbs the human mind, whereas a still mind enters right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
Only by severing all external conditions and stabilizing right mindfulness can quiescent wisdom arise, whereby one is finally able to clarify the principle.
Otherwise, though one may spend the entire day discussing the essence and explaining the teachings, in the end the Dharma will not enter the mind."
Master Yin said: "Master Dazhu said, 'When body, speech, and mind are pure, this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world;

when body, speech, and mind are impure, this is called the passing away of a Buddha. What is meant by 'Buddha' is not an external Buddha with physical marks, but rather the inherently present, numinous, and awakened nature within each person.
When the three karmas are pure, it manifests; when they are impure, it remains hidden."
Regarding those who are impure: they possess the ten non-virtuous actions through the three types of karma. There are three non-virtues of the body, namely:

killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. There are four non-virtues of speech, namely: false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech. There are three non-virtues of the mind, namely: greed, hatred, and delusion.

If these evils cease, they are immediately termed the ten wholesome actions. Because evil possesses the function of acting against one's nature, the Buddha-nature becomes hidden in accordance with it;
this is figuratively described as "nirvāṇa. Because the wholesome possesses the merit of acting in accordance with one's nature, the Buddha-nature manifests in accordance with it;
this is figuratively described as "transcending the world. Therefore, those who study the Way should constantly examine their three karmas.
"Do no evil; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the intent of all Buddhas.
Layman Shi Yun asked, "This mind is difficult to restrain; it does not rest day or night, racing about whether walking or sitting. What should be done about this?

The Master said, "This is the affliction caused by the mind, consciousness, and intellect (*citta-vijñāna-manas*). It should be treated precisely with the Buddha's knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*). — Yongjia.
It is said: "To damage the wealth of the Dharma and to extinguish merit—none of this fails to arise from this mind, consciousness, and awareness (*citta-vijñāna-manas*).

Therefore, the Gate of Meditation (*dhyāna-mukha*) brings the mind to an end, entering suddenly into the power of non-arising knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana-bala*). It is solely through the power of knowledge and vision that one can bring the mind to an end and enter into non-arising.

Since sentient beings have never been free from discursive thought (*vikalpa*) throughout beginningless eons, were it not for the power of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they would forever remain [in bondage]."
At the time of cessation, this Buddha-knowledge and vision is the sharp axe that truly cuts the root of afflictions and the swift vessel for crossing the ocean of birth and death;
it must not be abandoned for even a moment.
The Master said: "The deluded thoughts of sentient beings are immeasurable. Among them, those most entangling and difficult to resolve do not go beyond the two views of body and mind.

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: 'All sentient beings falsely recognize the four great elements as the characteristics of their own bodies, and the shadows of conditions from the six sense-objects as the characteristics of their own minds.
This is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky; yet in reality, there are no flowers in the sky—it is only the diseased eyes.'"

Those with deluded vision perceive flowers where none exist. The self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally devoid of body and mind. Those who are deluded regarding Perfect Enlightenment falsely identify the four elements and the six sense-objects as body and mind.
Therefore, throughout thousands of sutras and myriad treatises, there is an extensive refutation of these two views of body and mind.

Once these two views are shattered, the Buddha-nature manifests of itself. When the view of the body is shattered, the illusory body is itself the Dharma-body. When the view of the mind is shattered, then...

The illusory mind is itself the numinous and luminous Buddha-nature. This is what is meant by the statement that "the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature," and that "the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
The Seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, each transmitted the Dharma with a single verse, and every verse refutes the dualistic views of body and mind.
For instance, the verse of Vipaśyin Buddha says: "The body receives birth from within the formless; it is like..."
Just as illusions manifest various forms, the mind-consciousness of the illusionist is fundamentally non-existent; likewise, both sin and merit are empty and have no place of abiding.
"Formless" (animitta) refers to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Because it is not an object perceived by the mind, intellect, or consciousness, it is called formless.
This body arises within this formlessness by relying on causes and depending on conditions, just like an illusion. Since it is like an illusory manifestation, then...
The mind, intellect, and consciousness of an illusory person are fundamentally non-existent from the very beginning; it is not that they have been made non-existent.

Since the mind, intellect, and consciousness are absent, the good and evil, sins and blessings produced by them are merely like drifting clouds passing through the sky—coming from nowhere and going nowhere.
How could there be any place for them to abide or cling to? As the verse of Viśvabhū Buddha says: "Borrowing the four..."
The great elements are taken as the body. The mind is fundamentally without birth; it exists because of objects. If the preceding object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist.
Sin and merit are like illusions—they arise and they perish. As for the four great elements, they are earth, water, fire, and wind. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says:
"This body of mine is a combination of the four great elements—namely, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, impurities, and physical form—all of which..."
They return to earth. Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, spittle, foam, phlegm, tears, vital essence, and the large and small excretions all return to water.
Warmth returns to fire; movement returns to wind. When the four great elements each depart, where will this delusory body of today abide?
Thus, this very body ultimately has no substance; it exists as a manifestation of combination, truly identical to a magical illusion. (4)

Through the conjunction of conditions, the six sense organs falsely arise. The six sense organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally, and from within this accumulation of false conditioning-energies, there appears a semblance of objective phenomena;
this is conventionally named "mind. This delusory mind cannot exist without the six sense objects.
Viewed in this light, the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future are of one tongue and one roar. Body.
The body originally has no self-nature; it is merely a provisional borrowing of the four great elements to form a body.
The mind originally has no arising; it arises only through delusion due to external objects. If external objects do not exist, then the mind likewise cannot be apprehended.

Since the mind cannot be apprehended, how could the good and evil, or the offenses and blessings, that arise from it be apprehended? Therefore, it is said that there is "no place of abiding," because there is no dharma upon which one can abide.
During the Wanli era, the Elder Daguan spent his life preaching the Dharma and guiding others with this single verse alone.
He would say, "I, this old man, have only mastered the first two lines. If I were to master the latter two lines as well, then the two words 'birth and death' could do nothing to me.
He once instructed people to contemplate the body apart from the four elements, at which point he would say that this body is but the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.
To turn away from external objects and contemplate the mind alone, this mind is then but a mirage or a flower in the sky.
These words are all the more piercing; they must be understood with careful scrutiny. A verse by Kāśyapa Buddha says: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure;
from the beginning, it is unborn and cannot be extinguished. This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit. This verse—
This directly presents the nature of purity, which is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Body and mind are merely illusory manifestations;
within such illusory transformations, neither sin nor merit can be found. Compared with the preceding verses, this is even more poignant and clear.

The Master said: "An ordinary person of common ground has not yet attained the rank of a sage; who among them can be without fault? However, if one recognizes one's errors and reforms with repentance, no good deed could be greater.
If, on the other hand, one does not recognize one's errors, there will never be a day of reform and repentance, and one will continue to act according to one's whims, creating karma."
"One will not stop until one reaches the hells.
The Master said: "In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, from the very first opening of the mouth, it says:

'The continuous cycle of birth and death of all sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. They employ various deluded thoughts; these thoughts [do not...]"

"True. Thus there is cyclic existence. This means: if one knows that there is an eternally abiding true mind, then one need not employ various deluded thoughts, and there will be no cyclic existence of birth and death.
Since this eternally abiding true mind is something inherently possessed by every person, it is simply because they do not know it.
Because they do not know it, they conversely take the deluded for the true, thereby creating the karma of birth and death, with no day of escape from suffering.
Listen. It is like when a monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is the head? The worthy replied, "One must simply know that it exists. The monk asked, "What is the tail?
The worthy said, "Exhausting the present moment. This is because there must be a head before there can be a tail.
Even when the head and tail are fully complete, one must still know that there is a further point beyond.

The Master said: "When the Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared in the world, they established immeasurable Dharma-gates; there was nothing else they sought to do, but simply to cause people to realize that [the Truth] exists.
For instance, when the Patriarch Bodhidharma first came from the West and met Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked, 'What is the primary meaning of the holy truth?
The Patriarch replied, 'Vast emptiness—there is no holiness. One could say that the Patriarch Bodhidharma was truly cutting open the belly and gouging out the heart."
It was thus. However, Emperor Wu could not comprehend it; he still maintained the view of self and other, and said, "Who is it that stands before me?
The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. These two words, "I do not know," are something that no one in the entire world can overcome—except for those who truly know.
"It may be appropriate to reach a silent understanding beyond words.
The Master said: "One day Linji ascended the hall and said: 'There is a true person of no station who enters and exits through the gates of the faces of all of you.
Those of you who have not yet realized this, look! Look! Linji has already bought high and sold low; if you can grasp it..."
"Attained. Thus one knows that upon this mass of red flesh, it stands like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high; what more is there to seek regarding birth and death?
At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked, "What is the true person of no station? Linji seized him by the collar from his meditation seat and said, "Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
This may be called exhausting the master's compassionate heart to its limit—an immense kindness difficult to repay—but alas, this monk did not understand. Linji pushed him away.
Kaishan said: "The 'unranked true person'—what a dried-up dung-heap! When Linji arrived here, he once again manifested his three heads and six arms;
who could possibly catch up with him? An ancient worthy said: 'If there were no subsequent words, what would one have to seek in Linji?
How well he knew how to speak!"
The Master said: One day, while Yaoshan was sitting on a rock, Shitou asked him, "What are you doing here?
He replied, "I am not doing anything. Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are sitting idly. He replied, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something.
Shitou said, "You say you are not doing anything; what is it that you are not doing? He replied, "Even the thousand sages do not know it. Shitou [then departed].
The verse of praise says: "Living together from the beginning, we did not know his name; He proceeded spontaneously, simply walking along.
Even the sages of antiquity could not recognize him; How could ordinary people in their haste possibly understand him? The Master said:

"Yaoshan would not even accept this single word 'idle,' for he cut off the paths of both the mundane and the sage, seeing directly to the very root. It was no wonder that Shitou had to offer this praise."
Furthermore, if the great assembly wishes to know "existence," you need only recognize that which not even a thousand sages have recognized.
But how do you recognize that which not even a thousand sages have recognized? Not recognizing, not recognizing.
The Master said: "Once, while Yaoshan was seated, a monk asked him, 'Master, sitting there so motionless, what are you thinking about?
Yaoshan replied, 'I am thinking about that which cannot be thought. The monk asked, 'How can one think about that which cannot be thought? Yaoshan replied, 'It is not thinking.'"
The Master said: "This is precisely the shortcut method for practicing Chan meditation used by the ancients.
Ordinary people spend their days entirely within the realm of discursive thought; how could they know that they themselves inherently possess that which is beyond thought?
If you do know this, then from time to time, simply contemplate what the face of that which is beyond thought looks like. Contemplate it."
Reflect upon this. Reflect upon it again. Having reflected for a long time, you will suddenly attain awakening, like seeing the moon when the clouds part.
Only then will you know that this very act of reflection is fundamentally not reflection. In this way, one may be called a true master of reflection.
The Master said: Nanquan said, "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know that there is; the white oxen and black slaves, however, do know that there is.
The Master asked, "Why do the Buddhas of the three periods not know that there is? [Nanquan replied,] "It is simply because there is nothing to be known.

[The Master asked,] "Why, then, do the white oxen and black slaves know that there is? [Nanquan replied,] "Because they have never lost it. The mountain monk has now clearly explained this for you. Great!
Each family should examine this for themselves.

Layman Shi Yun asked, "The Buddha-dharma is vast and great; ultimately, through which gate does one enter? The Master said, "One enters through the gate of faith. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma: faith is that by which one enters; wisdom is that by which one [attains it]."

[The Buddha] crossed over [sentient beings]. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit. The Gate of the Patriarchs says: "Once one enters the gate of faith, one immediately ascends to the rank of the Patriarchs.

Because the World-Honored One did not speak falsely throughout many lifetimes, he received the retribution of the mark of the broad and long tongue; whenever he preached the Dharma, [he would extend it from his face to touch his forehead].
He extended his tongue to show it to people, manifesting that his words were trustworthy and free from falsehood; thus he said, "If the Buddha’s words are not believed, what words can be trusted?
That which is called faith consists of two things: first, faith in the Buddha’s words; second, faith in one's own mind. National Teacher Zhong said:
"Students of the Chan school must believe the Buddha’s words. Those of definitive meaning accord with the source of one's own mind, whereas those of non-definitive meaning do not."
I agree with you. It is like the worms within a lion’s body that eat the lion’s own flesh.
Those who do not believe the Buddha’s words today are not truly disbelieving the Buddha’s words; they are disbelieving their own minds.
The layman Mengsu asked, "I beg the Master to grant me an exposition on the principle of suffering and emptiness.

The Master said, "In the past, when the World-Honored One was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda asked the Buddha: 'After the World-Honored One has entered nirvāṇa, upon whom shall we rely? The Buddha told Ānanda:
'Whether in the present or in my past, rely upon the four foundations of mindfulness; do not rely upon anything else. These are the four foundations of mindfulness."
"Objects" (*āyatana*) refers to the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena. First, one contemplates the impurity of the body. There are five kinds of impurity:

first, impurity of the seed, which refers to the two drops of red and white from the father and mother; second, impurity of the dwelling place, which refers to the location within the mother’s womb, below the digestive organs and above the raw organs, like being in a latrine pit;
third, impurity of characteristics, which refers to the constant flow from the nine orifices; fourth, impurity of nature...
Impurity refers to the fact that its nature is impure; even when washed down to the level of minute particles, it remains foul and putrid.
Fifth is ultimate impurity, which refers to being cast away in a cemetery like a decayed log. Second is the contemplation of feeling as suffering. "Feeling" (vedanā) has the meaning of experiencing.

There are three kinds of sensation (*vedanā*): first, experiencing an adverse object gives rise to painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*); second, experiencing a favorable object gives rise to pleasant sensation (*sukhavedanā*);

third, experiencing a neutral object gives rise to equanimous sensation (*upekṣāvedanā*). Third, one contemplates that the mind is impermanent, meaning it is sometimes good and sometimes evil, arising and ceasing without pause.
The *Sutra on the Bequeathed Teaching* says: "The mind is more fearsome than a venomous snake, a ferocious beast, or a vengeful enemy. Great...

The fire escapes and spreads; it is insufficient as a metaphor. An ancient virtuous one said: "One should take the mind as one's teacher, not take the mind as one's teacher. Fourth, contemplate the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*):
this body consists only of the four great elements; there is no self within it. If even the body has no self, how much more so that which is outside the body?

Regarding these four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), constantly and diligently observe them with the power of wisdom; do not allow them to be forgotten for even a moment. This eliminates worldly...
Through craving, one swiftly realizes *nirvāṇa*.
The Master said: "The venerable teacher Wuming of Shouchang in Xujiang, whose name was Huijing, was the son of the Pei family of Chongren in Fuzhou."
He succeeded Master Zhong of Lingshan. While reading the *Transmission of the Lamp*, he encountered a monk asking Xingshan, "What is the Way?
to which Xingshan replied, "A truly fine mountain. Not understanding its meaning, he harbored doubts and engaged in arduous meditation.

One day, while lifting a stone, he attained sudden and great enlightenment. He spoke a verse, saying: "If you wish to study the unsurpassed path of Bodhi, Hasten to clear away this truly fine mountain. Once the Way is known..."
Only then did he realize that the mountain was not good; turning his body, he leaped out of the Patriarch’s Barrier. Dao-pai once composed a verse on this:

"Questioning the Way without cause, he was answered with 'a fine mountain'; The wooden man pushed him over, and he emerged from the heavy barrier. Now, rising up from the ground and soaring into the void, He remains as before amidst the vast, misty haze."
The Master said: "My senior teacher, Bozan Wuyi, whose name was Yu-lai, was the son of the Sha family of Shucheng.
One day, upon seeing someone climbing a tree, he attained great enlightenment. He went to visit Shouchang, who asked him, 'How have you been lately?
Bozan replied, 'There is a living path, but it simply must not be known by others. Shouchang asked, 'Why is it not known? Bozan replied, 'Because it is not known.'"
Knowing this, Dao-pai composed a verse: A single path of life is as slippery as moss; Swift-footed ones fly past, leaving not a speck of dust.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs have no secret formula to transmit; The dark-skinned fellow has attained it himself, his face filled with smiles.
The Master said: "My late teacher, the Elder Yongjue, whose name was Yuanxian, was of the Cai clan of Jianyang. Initially, upon hearing the story of Nanquan killing the cat, he attained realization.
He composed a verse and presented it to Shouchang, who told him to set it aside and engage in bitter meditation (*kukan*). One day, while reading the *Lotus Sūtra*..."
When he reached a secluded place where no one was present and was reciting this sutra, I then manifested for him a body of pure radiance.
Overjoyed beyond measure, he asked Chang, "What is this body of pure radiance? Chang stood up straight.
The Master said, "Is it only this, or is there something else besides? Chang then walked away. At that moment, the Master suddenly attained great enlightenment, as if a heavy burden had been lifted.

[The Master] said, "Failure. As [Chang] entered the abbot’s quarters, he reported what had transpired. Chang was suddenly struck with a staff three times, and [the Master] said, "Henceforth, you must not be careless.
He then showed him a verse, saying: "Each time one penetrates through, it becomes deeper; From of old, Buddhas and Patriarchs have not permitted others [to know].

Even if one were to leap upon the back of the Golden-Haired Lion, I would still require them to turn themselves around beneath the staff. The Master remained in doubt, wondering: "For what reason is there yet another need for the staff?"
He turned over his body [in death]. Four years passed. While passing through Yanjin, he heard a fellow monk chanting a sutra:
"At one time, they coughed and all together snapped their fingers; these two sounds reached throughout the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

He attained a vast and sudden enlightenment, penetratingly seeing the point of Shouchang’s application. Daopei composed a verse, saying: "A precious treasure fully laden, moored at Yanjin; on both banks..."
The scenery is exceptionally new. Ever since the fishing boat was overturned, Gautama has had no place to set down his idle body.
The Master said: "When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, there are two kinds of speech: first, speech according to their own intent; second, speech according to the intent of others.
As for speech according to their own intent: from the time the Tathāgata appeared in the world, everything he did was nothing other than for the sake of the one great cause."
This means that he intended to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
However, because sentient beings’ habitual tendencies were so thick and deep, they were unable to receive and uphold it; thus, he had no choice but to speak according to their inclinations.

He began at the Deer Park for the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, by turning the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths three times. The Four Noble Truths refer to suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path. Suffering and accumulation...
These are the causes and effects of the mundane world. Cessation and the Path are the causes and effects of the supramundane. As for the "three turnings," they are:
the turning of demonstration, the turning of exhortation, and the turning of realization. The turning of demonstration refers to: "This is suffering"—the characteristic of oppression.

This includes the suffering of pain in the desire realm, the suffering of change in the form realm, and the suffering of conditioned formations in the formless realm. "This is the origin"—the characteristic of summoning and inducing. This includes greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and the body.

[The truths of] suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are as follows: "This is suffering" refers to the view of a self, the view of extremes, attachment to precepts, attachment to ascetic observances, false views, and so forth.

"This is cessation" refers to the characteristic that can be realized: true reality, nirvana, which is free from all arising and ceasing. "This is the path" refers to the characteristic that can be cultivated:
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and so forth. Regarding the "turning toward exhortation," it means: "This is suffering; you should know it. This is the origin; you should abandon it."
"This is cessation; you should realize it. This is the path; you should cultivate it. Regarding the transformation through realization:
"This is suffering; I have known it, and shall not know it again. This is its origin; I have abandoned it, and shall not abandon it again.

This is its cessation; I have realized it, and shall not realize it again. This is the path; I have cultivated it, and shall not cultivate it again. Thus spoke Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the fifth of the [five] bhikṣus.
The Venerable Kāśyapa heard the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma and immediately severed both the afflictions of views and those of cultivation, realizing arhatship;

this is the Śrāvaka Vehicle. There are two types of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle. The first consists of those with sharp faculties who appear in a world without a Buddha; these are called Solitary Realizers (*pratyekabuddha*).

Dwelling alone on solitary peaks, they contemplate the dispersal and extinction of conditions and personally awaken to non-arising. The second type appears in a world where a Buddha exists; they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.

One who attains the Way is called a Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer). Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*): 1. Ignorance (*avidyā*). (Because one does not understand the ultimate truth, it is called ignorance.

2. Conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise. (Volitional formations refer to unwholesome actions, meritorious actions, and immovable actions. These two links are causes belonging to the past. 3. Conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises.

(Consciousness refers to the eighth *ālayavijñāna*. Drawn by volitional formations, it is the first to enter the womb. 4. Conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises. (The four aggregates of grasping that arise simultaneously with consciousness constitute name-and-form. 5. Conditioned by name-and-form...

6. The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). (This refers to the growth of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), resulting in the six [bases] and the eight [elements]. Consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases—these three links are all present during the fetal stage.

7. With the six sense bases as condition, contact (*sparśa*) arises. (This refers to the period after birth, gradually leading to maturity; the conjunction of the three factors—the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness—gives rise to contact. 8. With contact as condition, feeling (*vedanā*) arises. (This means that the experiencing of the object through contact constitutes feeling.

Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—these five links are the fruit and belong to the present life. 9. With feeling as condition, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises. (This means that attachment to feeling gives rise to craving. 10. With craving as condition, grasping (*upādāna*) arises. (This means that the intensification of craving is grasping. 11. With grasping as condition...

There is existence (*bhava*). (This refers to taking up outflowing karma (*āsrava-karman*) produced by grasping as existence. These three links—craving, grasping, and existence—are the causes for the future. Eleven: existence conditioned by grasping.

(This refers to the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) from karma as birth. Twelve: old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair conditioned by birth. (This means that the maturation of the aggregates is old age; the disintegration of the aggregates is death; the mental state is sorrow; weeping and wailing is lamentation; the five sense faculties are suffering; and the intensification of sorrow and suffering is despair.
The above twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) circulate through the three periods of time. It is due to these causal conditions that they accumulate.
There is no one who assembles [the causes]. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;

and so on, until with the cessation of existence, birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. It is through these conditions that they cease; there is no one who causes them to cease.

Thus, observing the characteristics of dependent origination in accordance with this sequence is the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. As for the Bodhisattva vehicle, it practices the six perfections, namely:

These are generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. The six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) transcend the six depravities: namely, generosity transcends stinginess and greed; ethical discipline transcends violation of precepts;
patience transcends anger and resentment; diligence transcends laziness; meditative concentration transcends distraction; and wisdom transcends ignorance.
These are the practices of the bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicle (upāyayāna). However, if one realizes that the self-nature is fundamentally devoid of stinginess and greed...
One practices the *dāna-pāramitā* in accordance with [the nature of reality], realizing that its self-nature is fundamentally free from transgression.
One practices the *śīla-pāramitā* in accordance with [the nature of reality], realizing that its self-nature is fundamentally free from anger.

One practices the *kṣānti-pāramitā* in accordance with [the nature of reality], realizing that its self-nature is fundamentally free from indolence. One practices the *vīrya-pāramitā* in accordance with...
Knowing that one’s own nature is fundamentally free from distraction, one practices in accordance with the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Knowing that one’s own nature is fundamentally free from delusion, one practices in accordance with the prajñā-pāramitā. Each and every pāramitā is thus in accord with one’s own nature;
there are no six pāramitās to be practiced apart from this nature. In this way, one is able to enter the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] with ease. This is...
This refers to the wondrous practice of non-action; this constitutes the Bodhisattva Vehicle. The Master said:
"One must understand the three causes of Buddha-nature. As for these three causes: the first is called the direct cause (zhengyin); the second is called the revealing cause (lioyin)."
The third is the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). As for the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*), it is the inherently existing nature of spiritual awakening possessed by all sentient beings.
As for the revealing cause (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*), it means that although sentient beings possess this nature, they have never realized it since beginningless eons;

it is only through the power of the revealing cause that one is able to perceive it. This is what is meant by: "It is not produced by a generative cause, but is only realized by a revealing cause. This is it.

As for the "causes and conditions" (pratyaya-hetu): once one has attained awakening, one should practice in accordance with the nature of reality through the six perfections and myriad practices, benefiting both oneself and others, so that merit and wisdom are perfected and the status of the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings is achieved.
The Master said: "A student of the Way must first investigate and clarify the fundamental source from which all phenomena arise.

If this foundation is clarified, one will naturally enter the Way without confusion. Formerly, before the World-Honored One appeared in the world, there were ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths in the West."
Each school champions its own tenets and treats others as slaves; they judge one another right and wrong like water and fire.

In sum, these views do not exceed two types: causelessness and false causes. To claim that something exists suddenly where there was nothing is called "causelessness"; such calculations are empty and erroneous.
This is called a false cause. There are those who reckon that all things are without cause and without condition, arising spontaneously and ceasing spontaneously;
for example, the black color of a crow is not due to dyeing, and the white color of a crane is naturally so. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there is a question:

"For what reason do those non-Buddhists give rise to the view of spontaneity? The answer is: "Because they observe the world as being without causes and conditions, or [seeing it] as occurring suddenly at times."

A great wind suddenly arises; at times it remains silent and still for a whole day, and at other times it suddenly causes violent sands to overflow, only to be instantly exhausted and cleared away in a single moment.
At times the trees stand dense and lush with blossoming fruit, and yet in another moment—
Suddenly becoming haggard and decrepit, it is because of this that such views arise, leading them to establish causeless theories (*ahetuvāda*).

Some reckon that the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), such as primordial darkness (*prakṛti*), give rise to all things; others reckon that they arise from the six categories (*padārtha*), namely substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*).
Some claim they arise from Mahābrahmā and so forth; others reckon that time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), space (*ākāśa*), and so on, are the causes.
The fundamental basis of both the world and nirvāṇa is precisely a false cause. This is analogous to the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism in this land:

Confucianism takes the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) as its cause, while Daoism takes spontaneity (*ziran*) as its cause. The *Daode jing* states: "Man models himself on the earth; the earth models itself on heaven; heaven models itself on the Way;
the Way models itself on spontaneity. The *Zhouyi* states: "In the *Yi*, there is the Great Ultimate; from it the Two Polarities are produced; the Two Polarities produce..."

"The four images give rise to the eight trigrams; the eight trigrams determine good fortune and misfortune; from good fortune and misfortune arise great undertakings," and so forth—all of this is not outside of this [principle].
If one were to claim that there is no cause, it would constitute a grave error. To say that things should not be produced would mean they must be produced constantly;
a barren woman should give birth to a child, a tortoise's hair should produce things, and without practicing the ten thousand practices, one should attain nirvana. Thus...

Both mundane and supramundane dharmas are simultaneously destroyed. If one calculates based on false causes, although such causes are not non-existent, because one does not realize that all is but mind, what is calculated is empty and erroneous;
the fault is likewise equal. When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, he established the correct causes and conditions, whereby all such calculations were shattered.

Regarding the primary causes and conditions: within the teachings for humans and devas, it is said that the two types of retribution—the primary (the physical body) and the secondary (the environment)—of the three realms and six paths all arise from the causes and conditions of karma.
In the Hīnayāna teachings, the six consciousnesses and the three poisons are regarded as the root of the mundane world. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"The three poisons give rise to the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind) through causes and conditions; the three karmas give rise to the three types of formations (namely, unwholesome actions, meritorious actions, and immovable actions) through causes and conditions."

Therefore, there exist all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). In the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, it is taught that there are eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), which are exclusively subject to arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
These establish the causes for both birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The element (*dhātu*) from beginningless time is the equal support of all phenomena;
from this arise the various realms of existence as well as the realization of nirvāṇa. Here, "element" (*dhātu*) has the sense of "cause," referring to the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*).

The consciousnesses established therein arise solely from karma and afflictions; True Suchness (*tathatā*) is quiescent, eternal, and immutable, and it is not permitted to undergo transformation according to conditions.

In the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-vyavasthāna*) of the Mahāyāna, the eight consciousnesses established therein are permeated by the Tathāgata-garbha and are established through following conditions. As a sutra says:
"The Buddha taught that the Tathāgata-garbha is the *ālaya-vijñāna*; they are mutually indistinguishable, like gold and a finger-ring. All...
Sentient beings are of one equal nature; they are merely *tathatā* (suchness) established according to conditions.

The Sudden Teaching does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) at all, but only distinguishes true nature. Furthermore, it lacks the distinctions of the eight consciousnesses;

everything that exists is merely deluded thought (*vikalpa*), and the entire *dharmadhātu* is beyond words. What is taught by the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle is solely the inexhaustible Dharma.
The realms. The nature-ocean is perfectly interfused; dependent origination is unimpeded, and so forth.
If one can proceed from the shallow to the deep, reaching the ultimate limit, one will know that all phenomena are the dependent origination of the nature-ocean—perfectly interfused and unimpeded.
One is all; all is one. Birth-and-death is nirvana; afflictions are bodhi. Equal, equal. Exhaustless, exhaustless.

It is not only the Sudden [teaching] of the beginning and end that is Perfect; even the Small Vehicle, the Human and Celestial realms, as well as Confucianism, Daoism, and the ninety-six types of heterodox paths from the Western Heaven, are all Perfect Teachings.
The Master said: "All Buddhas, sentient beings, mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all share the same Dharma-body as I. Can you all believe this?
Now, what is called the Dharma-body is precisely the self-nature inherently possessed by each person; it pervades the ten directions."
It encompasses all existence; one cannot see its head when approaching it, nor can one perceive its rear when following it.
It is high without a summit and deep without a bottom; it is boundless on the sides and non-existent in the center.
Pure and naked, clear and pristine, it is like empty space, containing all phenomena within it. It enters equally into all lands and abides nowhere among any realms.
Through discrimination, the mouth wishes to speak but words fail; the mind wishes to contemplate, yet thoughts vanish. Only those who have realized it can truly correspond with it.
Long ago, Master Xiaoshou was carrying firewood when he tripped and fell to the ground. Suddenly, he attained enlightenment and composed this verse:
"Striking down is not another thing; Spreading out is not mere dust. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth— All reveal the body of the Dharma King. Observe him!
The speech of one who has attained the bottom is how intimate! It is, directly beneath, like space merging with space; there is not a single crack or fissure.
If it were otherwise, you should believe the Buddha’s words—the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle—which accords with the source of one's own mind. For indeed, these are the Buddha’s words.
Each phrase is a phrase; each character is a character. It is true and not false; it is no idle talk. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body; they are one in mind and one in wisdom, and likewise in their powers and fearlessnesses.
This verse refers to the fact that all Buddhas are of the same essence. It further says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three..."
There is no distinction. This means that from the Buddhas above down to all sentient beings below, they share the same essential nature as one's own mind;

what difference could there be? Furthermore, it says: "The Dharmakāya pervades all places—all sentient beings and all lands throughout the three periods of time are entirely contained within it without exception, yet it has no form or characteristics by which it can be apprehended. This refers to this Dharmakāya.
Although no form or characteristic can be apprehended, it is identical with sentient beings, identical with the lands, and identical with the three periods of time.
Indeed, sentient beings, lands, and the three periods of time are the Dharma-body; the Dharma-body is sentient beings, lands, and the three periods of time.
Were there even a hair’s breadth that was not the Dharma-body, then the Dharma-body would have places where it does not pervade. Thus, Master Sengzhao said:
"Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things and I are one body. This also elucidates this very principle. Furthermore, it says:
"To take the myriad things as oneself—is this not the prerogative of the sage alone? When the Chan Master Shitou Xiqian read to this point, [he was deeply moved].
He then struck the desk and sighed, saying: "The Sage has no self; there is nothing that does not constitute his self. The Dharma-body has no form; who can speak of self and other?
Within this, the perfect mirror shines with spiritual brilliance. The myriad phenomena embody the profound mystery and manifest of themselves.
Since object and wisdom are not one, who can speak of coming and going? How sublime these words! This may be called a true understanding. If you gentlemen wish to understand..."
"All things are for oneself"—it is not at all improper to understand it in this way. Later, Shitou ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying:

"The Dharma-gate of my teaching was transmitted by the Buddhas of the past. It does not concern meditative concentration or diligent effort; it concerns only attaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. 'Mind is Buddha'—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings;
enlightenment, bodhi, and afflictions—though their names differ, their essence is one. You should all know your own self."
The mind is free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence; its nature is neither defiled nor pure. It is profoundly still and perfect, equal for both ordinary beings and sages.

Its applications are boundless, transcending the mind, intellect, and consciousness. The three realms and the six destinies are manifestations of one’s own mind alone; like the moon in water or images in a mirror, how could they have arising or ceasing?
If you can understand this, there is nothing that is not fully provided. That sentient beings today do not perceive the Dharmakāya is because their eyes—
Before you there are phenomena. You see your own body and mind; you see the three realms and the six paths of existence.
All these are merely making a living upon the skull. Therefore, the eye does not transcend form, and the ear does not go beyond sound.

If you can clearly realize that all phenomena are the manifestations of your own mind—like the moon in water or an image in a mirror, fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing—then this is what is called the Dharmakāya.
It is cool and serene; it is revealed in every single instance. At that time, a monk asked, "Who has attained the essential meaning of Caoxi?
Tou said, "One who understands the Buddha-dharma attains it. The monk asked, "Does the Master yourself attain it?
Tou said, "I do not. The monk asked, "Why do you not? Tou said, "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma. Observe how this ancient master delivered his words here.
Even this single word "understanding" admits of no room for conceptualization. Furthermore, a monk asked, "What is liberation?
Touzi said, "Who bound you? The monk asked, "What is the Pure Land? Touzi said, "Who defiles you? The monk asked, "What is nirvana?
Touzi said, "Who gave birth and death to you? If you can understand where Shitou lands, you will cut off both extremes and not dwell in the middle way.

It is granted that one may personally witness the Dharmakāya. The Dharmakāya realized by the Buddhas of the three periods of time is of one and the same essential nature as all Buddhas, sentient beings, mountains, rivers, and lands;
therefore, one is able to be fully endowed with the great compassion of identical substance (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*), such that the suffering of one is the suffering of all.

All joys and all forms of happiness throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space—wherever a single sentient being gives rise to a single thought—one knows them all completely and manifests one’s own body to rescue and deliver them.
Thus, a sutra says: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, appearing universally before all living beings;
responding to conditions and meeting with those who call, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi. If one can...
"One who has faith in the Buddha’s merits is a person endowed with great fortune and wisdom; such a person is no ordinary individual. The Master said:

"All Buddhas and sentient beings are equally endowed with the three bodies (trikāya) and the four wisdoms (caturjñāna). As for the three bodies, they are the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya), and the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
The Great Master the Sixth Patriarch said: 'The pure Dharma-body is your own nature; the perfect Reward-body is your..."
This is the wisdom [of the Buddha]. The thousands of billions of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are your practice. Buddhas and sentient beings share the same *dharmakāya*;
they are non-dual and without distinction. There are two types of the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya*: first, the body of self-enjoyment, which only Buddhas can know among themselves;
second, the body of enjoyment for others, which is the Buddha Vairocana, adorned with myriad virtues, for those on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The Bodhisattva who preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is this very one. As for the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it refers to what is said in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:
"At that time, Vairocana was seated upon a lotus pedestal; around him, upon a thousand petals, he further beheld a thousand Śākyamunis.
Within each petal were ten billion lands, and in each land was a Śākyamuni, each sitting beneath a bodhi tree and simultaneously attaining the Way of Buddhahood. This is it.

However, while the Buddhas have already realized this, sentient beings remain deluded; though its essence is inherently present, they do not recognize it in their daily activities. As for the four wisdoms, they are:

the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
When deluded, these become consciousnesses; when awakened, they become wisdoms. There are eight kinds of consciousness: first, the eye-consciousness; second, the ear-consciousness.
Third is the nose-consciousness; fourth is the tongue-consciousness; fifth is the body-consciousness; sixth is the mental-consciousness;

seventh is the manas-consciousness, which here is called the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*). This is the root of the six consciousnesses, as it is associated with self-delusion, self-love, and self-view.
The conceit of self (*asmimāna*) is associated with four afflictions. It grasps the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna* as an internal self;
it exclusively takes the internal as its object. The self-grasping of sentient beings is firm and solid, impossible to uproot; its root lies herein.

The eighth *ālaya-vijñāna* is here called the "store-consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*), because it possesses the three meanings of "store": first, it is "able to store," in that it can contain and store the sense faculties...

First, it is the "repository of seeds," because it contains the seeds of the body, the sense organs, and the external world. Second, it is the "that which is stored," because its own substance is stored within the seeds of the body, the sense organs, and the external world.

Third, it is the "repository of the attachment to self-love," because the *manas* consciousness clings to it as a self. It is also called the "fundamental consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*), because it serves as the foundation for the preceding seven consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it is called the "maturation consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*), because it can repay the karmic results produced by the sixth consciousness.

Regarding the two types of karma—projecting and completing—one is reborn according to their respective categories because they ripen at different times, ripen as different natures, and ripen as different classes.
As for the transformation of wisdom: the *ālaya-vijñāna* is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; the *manas-vijñāna* is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality;
the sixth *mano-vijñāna* is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; and the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing [Activities].

Regarding the wisdom of what is done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*): consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) fundamentally do not possess two distinct natures; there is only the difference between delusion and awakening.

Sentient beings employ consciousness, while Bodhisattvas employ wisdom. When the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Four Reliances," instructs one to rely on wisdom and not on consciousness, it is precisely to effect the merit of this transformation.
The Master said: "Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been obscured from their numinous, luminous, and vast intrinsic nature.
They falsely identify the four elements as the body and seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as the mind. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

'It is like casting aside hundreds of thousands of clear and tranquil oceans, yet recognizing only a single bubble and calling it the entire tide; to exhaustively measure the vast seas while doing so is truly to be pitied.'"
As for these four great elements, they do not exceed a single skull. Though one moves, sits, comes, goes, speaks, and makes sounds, it is like a wooden puppet operated by mechanisms;
when the strings are severed, it ceases. As for seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they do not exceed a single shadow conditioned by the six sense objects.
Though one hears sounds and sees forms, appearing vivid and luminous, they are like the moon reflected in water, which immediately vanishes.
Wandering and surging, the eyes receive a body due to karma; the body, in turn, creates karma. From the mind, objects arise; from objects, the mind is further produced.
Intertwined and entangled, there is no way to escape. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "These ordinary beings are ignorant and without wisdom; they are truly to be pitied.
They have had countless bodies that have already perished, are now perishing, and will perish. Though they have thus utterly perished, they are unable to [attain liberation]."
Though they experience revulsion toward the body, they further increase the suffering of the mechanical apparatus; they follow the stream of birth and death and cannot turn back.
They do not seek escape from the house of the aggregates (*skandha*), nor do they recognize the fear and anxiety of the four great poisonous snakes.
They are unable to extract the arrows of pride and views, nor can they extinguish the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor destroy the darkness of ignorance.
Enveloped in darkness, they are unable to dry up the great ocean of craving and desire. Failing to seek the Great Sage Guide endowed with the ten powers, they enter the dense forest of Māra’s intent.
Within the ocean of birth and death, they are adrift and submerged by the waves of discursive thought and reflection. Such are these sentient beings.
They undergo such suffering—lonely, destitute, and oppressed; without rescue or reliance, without an island or a shelter, without refuge or eyes, shrouded by ignorance and enveloped in darkness.
For the sake of all those sentient beings, I now practice the dharmas of merit, wisdom, and the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Alone, I give rise to this resolve, seeking no companion. By these merits, may all sentient beings...
It is ultimately pure, even unto the attainment of the Tathāgata’s ten powers and unimpeded wisdom.

Now, when a bodhisattva resolves to deliver sentient beings, they first cause them to see through and break down this body. Once the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is broken, the view of a mind will break of its own accord without being deliberately targeted.
Long ago, there was a man who stayed alone in an empty pavilion. At midnight, he saw a ghost holding a skull.
When they arrived, a second ghost followed after them. The two ghosts each contended, claiming, "This corpse is mine!
As their dispute did not cease, they asked a person, "By whom was this corpse brought here? The man reflected, "These two ghosts are fierce and evil; it would be better not to speak the truth."
He then pointed to the first ghost and said, "That one brought him here. The second ghost was greatly enraged and tore off one of the man's hands to eat it.
The first ghost said, "This is my fault for bringing you trouble," and then tore off one of his own hands to replace the man’s.

After the second ghost had torn off and eaten every part of the corpse until nothing remained, he raised his hand to wipe his mouth and departed. The first ghost restored the corpse limb by limb. At dawn, the man awoke.
His mind was frantic and agitated. He went as far as the Jeta Grove, where he saw various bhikṣus and asked them, "Do I have a body?
From one monastic cell to another, he asked this very same question. A certain venerable one said, "This man knows that there is no body."
"You may now cross over. He then said to him, "Originally you had no body; it was merely by borrowing the four great elements that you took on a body.
Upon hearing this, the man attained great awakening and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
The layman Chen Weigong said: "The mandate of Heaven, profound and unceasing—this is the fundamental substance of the mandate of Heaven.
What Heaven mandates is called 'nature'—this is the mandate of Heaven flowing forth and reaching all things. The Master said: "This is also one interpretation.

However, the character for 'nature' (xing) seems to explain it too superficially. I, the humble one, say that the two characters 'Heaven's mandate' (tianming) are precisely [the meaning of] the 'profound and unceasing' in the original poem."
"The mandate of Heaven descends, profound and unceasing. "Profound" refers to Heaven; "unceasing" refers to the mandate.

The three characters "its" (之), "nature" (性), and "is" (謂) are the explanatory glosses of Master Zisi. He means that the mandate of Heaven is precisely the wondrous nature shared by both ordinary beings and sages.
All people and the sages alike possess this same single nature; it is only that ordinary people turn their backs upon it and act falsely.
In daily life, people are unaware [of this]. Sages and worthies exhaust their potential to return to the source; they follow their nature to give rise to function.
If one can cultivate according to the Way, forgetting emotional attachments to merge with one's nature, then even ordinary people can attain the state of sages and worthies.

The layman Wei Gong said, "Zhouzi [Zhu Xi] took 'stillness' (jing) as his principle, while Cheng [Yi] and Zhu [Xi] took 'reverence' (jing) as their principle; these are the essential keys for transcending the mundane and becoming a sage," and so forth.
The Master said, "Stillness and reverence are the subtle truths of the Confucian school. The Song scholars grasped them and presented them to others, expounding upon them with great effort;
they are most intimate and direct. Even the methods for entering the Way of the Buddhists—how could they possibly be outside of these? If one wishes to clarify this further..."

One attains the fundamental essence of stillness and reverence; it is like felling a tree by reaching its root, or treating an ailment by finding the correct acupuncture point—in both cases, the efficacy is verified immediately upon application.
As the ancients said, "Only after studying Buddhism does one truly understand Confucianism. How could these words deceive anyone?

However, those who are now beginners in the Buddha-dharma should first enter deeply through a single gate rather than attempting to coordinate every detail with another tradition. If one indeed develops a profound faith in the Buddha-dharma...
With right faith, investigate thoroughly and exhaustively until there is a sudden, penetrating realization.

Then, not only will stillness and reverence accord with the Buddha-dharma, but throughout the Four Books and Five Classics, there will not be a single sentence or a single word that is not the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) of the Buddha-dharma.
Answering the Three Questions of Layman Cheng Mo’an:

The first question asks: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said, "A bodhisattva practicing the path should not renounce the world in this manner—by cutting off body hair and head hair, and donning dyed saffron robes.
Rather, one should cut off afflictions and eliminate the greed, hatred, and delusion of all sentient beings."
To merely renounce the world and dwell in solitude, possessing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) alone, is not true renunciation.

To gather in beings of evil conduct and establish them in wisdom—that is called renunciation. To seek one’s own delight in diligence and strive for *nirvāṇa* for oneself alone is not true renunciation.
To exhort and transform sentient beings, first seeking with a firm mind for the sake of all beings—that is called renunciation.
The path leading to Nirvana is what is called "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*). If this is indeed the case, what distinction is there between living at home and leaving home?
The World-Honored One must have established the rule of tonsure; where, then, does the difference lie?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has said that one may dwell together with all gods, Brahmās, kings, ministers, and the assembly of Brahmins, but only with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
They are not true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); you must not go with them. When we have left the household life, whom should we serve? The Master replied:

"The Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) discuss leaving the world in terms of their outward traces; thus, they define 'leaving the household life' as cutting off hair and beard, dyeing the robes, and donning the saffron kashaya.
The Bodhisattvas, however, discuss entering the world in terms of their inner mind; thus, they define it as cutting off the afflictions (kleśa) and eliminating the suffering of all sentient beings."

To leave the household life is to take form as the object of greed, anger, and delusion; if one attains mastery over the mind, then whether one shaves the hair or keeps it, whether one remains at home or leaves the household, there is nothing acceptable and nothing unacceptable.

If one merely clings to outward appearances, then not only is the shaving of the body’s hair and the wearing of dyed robes not the essence of leaving the household life, but one would also cling to the words regarding the severing of afflictions while neglecting the regulations for shaving the hair and dyeing the robes.
Nor is this true renunciation. Those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are intent on self-benefit;
therefore, they regard the observance of the complete precepts, dwelling alone in tranquility, and seeking nirvāṇa as their renunciation. Bodhisattvas, however, are intent on benefiting others;

therefore, they regard the gathering of evil sentient beings and causing them to abide in wisdom, and even first seeking the path to nirvāṇa for the sake of all sentient beings, as their renunciation.
One leaves the household life. If one truly gives rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna, then even before having attained deliverance for oneself, one first delivers sentient beings;

this merit of benefiting others is itself self-benefit. As for the statement that "all devas, Brahmā kings, ministers, and assemblies of Brahmins may dwell together," it is because the nature of the consciousness of ordinary beings is not fixed, and they can still give rise to the resolve [for enlightenment]. This refers to what is called the low-lying, muddy sludge.
This refers to the blooming of the lotus flower. It is precisely because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) that one must not dwell with them;
for those fixed in the nature of the Two Vehicles cannot give rise to the Bodhicitta. This is what is meant by the saying: "In high ground and dry land, the lotus flower does not grow.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* does not permit associating with those of the Two Vehicles, whereas the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* speaks of those who turn their backs on the Great Vehicle and incline toward the Small.

Furthermore, one should even briefly contemplate the precepts of the Hīnayāna; for I truly fear that through long-term intimacy, one may become tainted by the narrow and inferior habits of the two vehicles.
The second question asks: While the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion mixed within the mind are truly to be feared, why does a Bodhisattva greedily grasp at the Great [Vehicle]?

Attachment is also a poison; failing to cultivate patience when provoked by anger is also hatred; and attempting to transform those who are difficult to transform over hundreds or thousands of lifetimes is also delusion.
How could these three poisons not constitute poisons within the sphere of a Bodhisattva? Yet, regarding these three, which defilements are light and which are heavy?
Which come first and which come last? Which may be transgressed and which may not? Which can be removed and which cannot? [The text begins: Attachment...

Desire arises from longing; when longing is stilled, it ceases. Anger arises from resentment; when resentment flares up, it increases. Ignorance is rooted in one's nature; when that nature is deluded, it becomes fixed.
