For those who would cultivate the Way, emotions may be removed, but nature cannot be forcibly altered. How should one proceed? The Master replied:
"The three poisons of sentient beings are rooted in emotional consciousness, whereas the three poisons of a Bodhisattva arise from wisdom and compassion. Comparing these two...

If one evaluates this from the standpoint of the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust is established; in that case, even wisdom and compassion would be termed "poison.
Compared with the perspective of emotional consciousness (*vijñāna*), the difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth—how could they possibly be discussed as being on the same level?

As for the claim that emotion can be eliminated while nature cannot be forcibly altered, this refers to one's innate endowment and habitual tendencies, not the true nature (*dharmatā*). This is because the true nature is free from conceptual thought (*niṣprapañca*).
It is fundamentally pure; since wisdom and compassion are themselves unattainable, how much more so are emotional consciousnesses?
To claim that emotional consciousness can be eliminated before one has yet perceived true nature is likewise nothing but empty talk.
The third question asked: "Wěi was by nature dull and slow-witted from childhood; stubborn, ignorant, and obstinate, he did not believe in the Buddha Vehicle.

Yet, in his dreams, he would sometimes ascend to the heavens, composing verses and offering praise; or he would be in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, prostrating before Buddhist stupas and seeing countless towers;
or he would walk upon Jade Mountains. His dreams were also frequently miraculous, being verified either by the passage of time or by immediate circumstances."

Regarding matters from long ago, there is nothing that does not accord with the accounts of his words and deeds. Lately, while reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā* during the day, I have been unable to avoid having dreams;
I am already overcome with shame and remorse. Furthermore, many of these visions are not auspicious. At times, my actions are entirely contrary to my intentions:
I may enter a royal palace and find myself sporting with consorts and handmaidens, only to experience great terror; or I may become a great general.
He led armies and commanded battle arrays, killing countless people. At times he went to the land of the rākṣasas to seek out his own offspring;
at other times he boarded great ships and entered the vast waters of the great ocean, drifting for an infinite duration. Or he entered hell, where he was rebuked by King Yama.
Furthermore, he prostrated and offered praises to the King, yet he ate meat and violated the precepts, reaching such extremes that there was nothing he would not do.
Is this dream-vision perhaps because the power of the Way is not firm? Or is it because the habitual tendencies accumulated over many lifetimes have not yet been forgotten?

Or could it be due to some other omen or prophecy? "Please resolve my confusion," [the King] requested. The Master replied: "A dream is a mental construction. It arises from the seeds of *prajñā* accumulated over many lifetimes."

If one’s mind is not pure and unified, but is instead cluttered with delusive thoughts, these will manifest in dreams; moreover, they may vary in many ways according to good or evil, favorable or adverse conditions.
If the power of the Way is not firm, the habitual tendencies accumulated over many lifetimes—such as the portents of others' prophecies—will all appear.
If you can suddenly open the eye of right vision and penetrate to the source of nature, then dream-thoughts will be severed and the great dream will awaken. *Buddha* (in Sanskrit).
"Tuo" (Buddha) means "the Awakened One. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Buddha-mind has no other; perfect awakening awakens the world. This is what that refers to.

It is said, "The ultimate person has no dreams," which is indeed true. Yet, if so, how do you account for the Buddha dreaming of the golden drum and Confucius dreaming of placing his tablet between the two pillars?
The Master said: "To call him 'Buddha' or to call him 'Confucius'—that is already a dream."
"How much more so for the golden drum between the two pillars? The questioner nodded and withdrew.
"Coming from the Center" is the primary principle of the Five Ranks; it is the pivot of the five positions. The first two ranks are those who enter into this; the latter two ranks proceed from it.
This is "Emergence from the Center" (Zhèngzhōngpiān). It is established in reference to the initial moment of awakening. Principle (*lǐ*) is the center; awakening (*wù*) is the deviation.

Therefore, there is the phrase, "Do not be surprised that we meet yet do not recognize one another," which still harbors the lingering resentment of former days. This is "Deviation within the Center" (Piānzhōngzhèng).
This is established at the time of "transferring merit to the station. Primarily, this concerns merit; the station is the primary reality. Thus it is said:

"Clearly face-to-face, there is nothing else true; do not further lose your head by still recognizing its reflection. One must urgently exert oneself to gather the partial back into the primary, striving with all one's might to push the father into the interior.
Within the single station of "coming from the midst of the primary," there are three parts. The first half involves transferring merit while one has not yet reached the station.
The stage is merely a realm of singular color. Next, once that singular color has dissolved, one returns to the true position (*zhengwei*), the pinnacle of nobility, which must not be violated.
As it is said in the teachings: "This is the stage of learning (*xuewei*), not the stage of realization (*zhengwei*);

therefore, one must turn back from within it and is not permitted to dwell in attachment. In the latter half [of the process], one has already turned back from within the stage to apply oneself to merit, yet still...

"Before it has united with the sensory realm"—this refers to what is called "the path within non-existence being separated from dust. Tong'an said: "As soon as one puts on soiled robes, one claims to be a Buddha;
yet when one dresses in precious regalia, who is it that is named? He also said: "The wooden man goes out at midnight wearing boots;
the stone woman returns at dawn wearing a cap. All these express this same meaning. The ancient masters established the five minor positions (*wuwei*) and...
The four transformations of the spiritual mechanism are all established for this purpose. Indeed, this single stage is difficult to enter initially;
once entered, it is even more difficult to turn the body from within the stage. If one has not yet entered this, one remains a common worldling of the broad ground.
If one has entered but cannot turn the body, and instead seeks realization therein, one will fall into the two vehicles. Try reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle... [text truncated]
The eighth stage can thus be understood. "Simultaneous Middle Reaching" (jiānzhōng zhì) is established when both function and position are manifested together;
"Simultaneous Middle Arriving" (jiānzhōng dào) is established when both function and position are simultaneously extinguished. This is the general meaning. Let us now cease this prolixity.
Upon hearing that I had discussed the principles of the Five Ranks with Master Shichao, the Zen practitioner Kaehwa was filled with great joy.
He presented paper and requested that I write something for him; I have therefore set forth its general outline here. Once you have finished reading it, you may consign it to the flames.
A Proclamation for the Prohibition of Catching Yellow Frogs: The yellow frogs of Mount Bai Zhang belong to the species of *maṇḍūka*.

Every time spring arrives, males and females come forth in great numbers, filling the fields and blocking the roads. They do so only with the aim of producing sons and daughters, unaware that they must avoid death and seek safety.
When they were born, the villagers knew nothing of them; they vied with one another to seize and eat them, as easily as if they were picking up pebbles.
They severed their heads and flayed their skins; they cut open their entrails and hacked their flesh until blood flowed across the ground, no different from human blood.

The heads are piled into a mound; how do they differ from human heads? The killer does not realize that the suffering is unbearable, nor does the eater take pity on the fact that the resentment reaches the heavens.
It is said that in the past, Huang Chao once gathered his troops here to plunder and slaughter the lives of the people, and thus such a retribution was incurred.
Indeed, to kill a person and then be killed by another is a cause and effect that leaves no room for error. [This applies even to] eating clams...
They then transform themselves into frogs, repaying their debts without fail; this extends even to oxen, sheep, dogs, pigs, chickens, geese, ducks, pigeons, and fish.
Turtles, loaches, eels, shrimp, clams, crayfish, crabs, conches, and snails—indeed, any living creature that is killed and eaten.

Their confession and reporting are exactly like that of Huang Chao regarding the yellow shells; they are one and the same without distinction. Life after life, they remain constantly in the cycle of transmigration;
generation after generation, there is no means by which to attain liberation. If one does not rely on the power of the Triple Gem, how can the transgressions accumulated over kalpas be released?

In the winter of the Guiwei year of the Chongzhen era, while I was dwelling in seclusion on this mountain, I once gathered my fellow practitioners to perform repentance on their behalf for more than twenty [days].

For many years, these creatures had vanished from sight. Yet in recent times, they have once again become numerous. The younger generation, following their old habits, vie with one another to capture and eat them.
They do not consider the suffering of death that others endure, caring only for the sweet taste that satisfies their own tongues. This is entirely because they have not encountered the Buddha-dharma;

they do not believe in cause and effect, nor do they understand the nature of sin and merit. Thus they commit this act of killing, sowing the seeds for suffering in both the present life and future existences.
This is endless suffering. Now, in the autumn of the Xinhai year of the Kangxi era, I traveled once more to Zhicheng.
I specially invited various virtuous friends to emulate the events of the Guiwei year, so that both those who catch clams and those who eat them might together offer repentance.

It is my hope that the Buddha’s light will shine through clearly and his spiritual power will provide secret aid, so that the malevolent intent of those who catch clams may be instantly stilled, and they shall no longer consume clam meat.

May we avoid falling into the body of a clam. For those who have been clams, may their nature of wisdom increase and become luminous; may they not harbor vengeful retribution and forever transcend the realm of clams.

May they regard one another with eyes of compassion, free from any intent to kill or harm. May they ascend together to the Dharma assembly, where both people and things enjoy the joy of kindness and kinship.
May they aspire to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) and ultimately realize Bodhi—this is our aspiration. We pray only that those of high wisdom will turn [the wheel of Dharma].
Exhorting one another toward transformation, their merit is unsurpassed.
Layman Weiwu Li has reached the age of fifty;

I, Yuyu, have come to Bailing (White Cloud) in Fusha to oversee the construction of the Precious Hall for the Awakened Sovereign. It is an honor that the great elder, Master Weiwu Li, has graced this endeavor.

He practiced the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), and his merit was fully realized; moreover, he would frequently urge his horse to visit me, discussing the Way and conversing on the mind with tireless persistence.
It is evident that he had long possessed the causal conditions for *prajñā*. That we met by chance this once was no mere accident.

This year, on the nineteenth day of the tenth month in the winter of the Xinhai year, coinciding with the auspicious moment when the Master’s great *da-yan* (great calculation) reached the number nine, I reflected that there was nothing else I could offer for his longevity.
Thus, I have composed these crude words and present them to express my sincere devotion. I have heard it said by the ancient masters:
"Blessings are observed in one's capacity; longevity is observed in one's use of mind. This means that the magnitude of one's blessings corresponds to the breadth of one's capacity.

The presence or absence of this [virtue] is seen in one's perspective; the thickness or thinness of one's application of mind is seen in the longevity of life and the abundance or scarcity of its fruits.

Your Lordship’s capacity encompasses both gratitude and resentment, harmonizing those above and below. It is vast and expansive, like a ten-thousand-acre expanse of the dark blue ocean—stirred yet not turbid, poured into yet not overflowing;
it receives the hundred rivers and gathers all waters. As for such a capacity, how could it be compared to that of a mere mountain stream or brook?
The capacity of a basin-like pond can be measured and known. Since the Master’s measure is such, how could the depth and breadth of his merit and virtue have any limit?
As for the Master’s application of mind: though his body dwelt amidst the toil of the mundane world, his heart roamed beyond all phenomena.

He sought the Way among the mountains and widely established bridges and rafts, truly possessing the spirit of Vimalakīrti and Lao Pang. His construction of Buddha images, his feeding of the Sangha, and his printing of [scriptures]...
The assembly of the economic order has all been made public through your wondrous deeds.
Since your mental application is so diligent in this regard, how could your lifespan be measured? You are now precisely at the age of fifty, when one knows their destiny;
you are like the blazing sun at its zenith, illuminating the entire world. Thus, both I and you are together wandering within the Great Radiant Treasury of the Tathāgata.
They acted as hosts and guests to one another, mutually stimulating and uplifting each other.
In every word and silence, every movement and stillness, there was nothing that did not serve to illuminate, circulate, and exalt the *Śūraṅgama* Sūtra.

How could this be compared to the worldly calculations of longevity for turtles and cranes, or the conventional discourse on the rising sun and waxing moon? As for the formless Dharma-body and its immeasurable lifespan, its roots...
Encompassing the primordial state of heaven and earth, its radiance surpasses that of the sun and moon; thus, you have already attained silent resonance beyond words.

This cannot be fully exhausted by mere brush and tongue; I shall briefly describe your noble magnanimity and your dedication to benefiting others through goodness, as a prognostication for your great fortune and long life.

Master Yuan resided at the foot of Mount Lu. He was rigorous and austere in observing the Vinaya; he would not accept honeyed broth after midday. He composed poems to exchange for wine to drink with Tao Pengze.
When seeing off guests, regardless of their rank—whether noble or humble—he would never cross the Tiger Creek. Yet, he did cultivate friendship with the Daoist Master Lu.
Jingxing walked over a hundred paces across the stream, laughed heartily, and took his leave. Chan Yue wrote a poem that says: "I love Official Tao, staggering in his drunkenness;
I see Daoist Lu walking slowly as he departs. Buying wine and crossing the stream—both are breaking the precepts.
Who is this person? This Master is such a one. Song dynasty Huang Luchi wrote a poem that says: "Inviting Tao Yuanming to hold the wine cup, Seeing off Lu Xiujing as he goes."
Passing beyond Tiger Creek, the nine schools of thought within his breast were as clear as a mirror; amidst the myriad affairs of the human world, he was as oblivious as one drunk in the mud.
I have ventured to emulate him, saying: "In the midst of love and intoxication, he was able to achieve deep introspection; among those who differ from Lu, there is still common ground.
Exchanging wine and crossing the bridge, he removed the wedge with a wedge, truly causing posterity for a thousand ages to look up to his lofty wind."
Preface to the Twelve Poems on Shadows by Huang Yuzhen:
Heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all, in their entirety, shadows. All people in the world are but men who toy with shadows.
Little do they realize that form is the source of shadow and that shadow arises from form; yet they seek shadow within shadow, thereby falling ever further into error.
Master Huang Gongyu-zhen lived in seclusion within a village. As he was advanced in both years and virtue, his vision remained keen.
He thus composed the "Poems on the Twelve Shadows. To speak of those closest at hand, I have made them easy to understand.
If readers can seek the shadows through these poems, and seek that which is not the shadow through the shadows, then this work by Master Yu will truly provide profound benefit.

These are but idle words. If one merely lingers over the wind and moon, or indulges in the composition of phrases and characters, then the sword has long since departed while one is still mending the boat.
I, too, cannot help but sigh over this "playing with shadows."

Preface to the *Erveng Zhizhuyue* (The Finger-Moon of Rhymes and Phonetics). The method of rhyming through *fanqie* (phonetic analysis) originated among the followers of Śākyamuni. In my youth, I was the misfortune of entering their ranks, yet I had never previously given a thought to the study of phonology.
One day, Huang Zijiuyu presented to me his compilation, the *Yunfa Hengtutu Yinqie Zhizhuyue*, and requested a preface.
First, as for unfolding the scroll, it is like a tiger staring at a waterwheel; one cannot perceive its seams or gaps at all.
How, then, could a preface be composed? Nevertheless, I have heard from National Teacher Qingliang that the *mātṛkā* (mother-letters) are the root of all characters.

Just as with the thirty-four letters such as ka, kha, ga, and gha, when the twelve vowels such as sa (high tone), sa (level tone), si, and sri are applied to these thirty-four letters, each single letter becomes twelve letters.
Furthermore, through combinations of two, three, and even up to six, all other letters are produced;
